runs.t: So, are we done with virtualization?
Hey, no reason to get so excited; I was just asking a question. Students are supposed to do that, right?
Well, professors do always say that, but really they mean this: ask questions,
you have actually put a little thought into them.
Well, that sure takes the wind out of my sails.

Mission accomplished. In any case, we are not nearly done with virtualization! Rather, you have just seen how to virtualize the CPU, but really there is a big monster waiting in the closet: memory. Virtualizing memory is complicated and requires us to understand many more intricate details about how the hardware and OS interact.
That sounds cool. Why is it so hard?

Well, there are a lot of details, and you have to keep them straight in your head to really develop a mental model of what is going on. We’ll start simple, with very basic techniques like base/bounds, and slowly add complexity to tackle new challenges, including fun topics like TLBs and multi-level page tables. Eventually, we’ll be able to describe the workings of a fully-functional modern virtual memory manager.
Neat! Any tips for the poor student, inundated with all of this information and generally sleep-deprived?
For the sleep deprivation, that’s easy: sleep more (and party less). For understanding virtual memory, start with this:
every address generated by a user program is a virtual address

. The OS is just providing an illusion to each process, specifically that it has its own large and private memory; with some hardware help, the OS will turn these pretend virtual addresses into real physical addresses, and thus be able to locate the desired information.
OK, I think I can remember that... (to self) every address from a user program is virtual, every address from a user program is virtual, every ...
Oh nothing.... (awkward pause) ... Anyway, why does the OS want to provide this illusion again?
: the OS will give each program the view that it has a large contiguous

to put its code and data into; thus, as a programmer, you never have to worry about things like “where should I store this variable?” because the virtual address space of the program is large and has lots of room for that sort of thing. Life, for a programmer, becomes much more tricky if you have to worry about fitting all of your code data into a small, crowded memory.
are big deals, too. We don’t want one errant program to be able to read, or worse, overwrite, some other program’s memory, do we?
Probably not. Unless it’s a program written by someone you don’t like.
Hmmm.... I think we might need to add a class on morals and ethics to your schedule for next semester. Perhaps OS class isn’t getting the right message across.
Maybe we should. But remember, it’s not me who taught us that the proper OS response to errant process behavior is to kill the offending process!
